en: The Dīrgha Āgama, Daśottara-sūtra, Volume I, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time,
The Venerable Śāriputra said:

"I request that the bhikṣus listen to the teaching of the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is endowed with wisdom and skill, and is the most complete, pure, and ultimate exposition of practice. Listen to the ten dharmas, increasing from one to ten; listen with focused attention and heedfulness, and listen to the teaching as it is spoken."
The bhikṣus said to the Venerable Śāriputra,
“We pray that you will grant us the opportunity to hear it.
Śāriputra replied:
He then explained that from the arising of the first [factor] up to the ten dharmas, they all aggregate to form the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
From suffering, one attains the essential exit, whereby all afflictions are extinguished.
Regarding the "first single dharma," the practitioner ultimately achieves the unconditioned by simply maintaining their practice.
“The second single dharma is that one should contemplate how the mind does not depart from the body.
The third single dharma is that one should discern the coarse and subtle aspects of the world.
The fourth single dharma is that one should abandon conceit.”
"The fifth single dharma is that which can be focused upon as the primary object of contemplation.
The sixth single dharma is that which is frequently practiced as the primary object of contemplation.
The seventh single dharma is the attainment of the concentration of non-interruption, which is difficult to experience."
"The eighth single dharma is that which can bring about the establishment of mindfulness.
The ninth single dharma is that one should know all people subsist on food.
The eleventh dharma is that one should realize it so that the mind has no doubt."

"These ten qualities of the practitioner are not false, not otherwise; they are true and such as they are, unconfused and non-perverted. They are to be observed by one who possesses wisdom and maintains right mindfulness."
"The first pair of dharmas: the practitioner should ultimately be without action, yet should maintain intention and mindfulness.
The second pair of dharmas: one may increase both tranquility and insight."
"The third pair of dharmas should be understood as names.
The fourth pair of dharmas consists of delusion and worldly craving, which are to be abandoned.
The fifth pair of dharmas consists of lack of shame and lack of remorse, which are to be eliminated."
"The sixth pair of dharmas: it is difficult to determine that these two dharmas should not be thus.
"The seventh pair of dharmas: one should know that these two dharmas should not be thus.
"The eighth pair of dharmas: they may be sought as the point of exhaustion, the point of non-arising."

"The ninth pair of dharmas: one should recognize what causes and conditions lead a person to experience suffering while in the world, and one should also know what causes and conditions lead to liberation from the world.
The tenth pair of dharmas: one should personally realize wisdom and also attain liberation."

These are the twenty dharmas for the practitioner; they are not otherwise, not different, possessing realization as it truly is, and being neither deluded nor inverted—this is the contemplation of the mind with wisdom as it truly is.

"The first set of three dharmas: when a practitioner has completed the task of wisdom regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they should both hear the discourses on the Dharma and contemplate the fundamental source.
The second set of three dharmas: one should practice reflection."
Regarding desire: one neither desires nor attends to it.
"The third set of three phenomena should be known:
existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm."
“The fourth set of three things to be abandoned:
sensual desire, desire for form, and desire for the formless.
“The fifth set of three things to be abandoned:”
There are three fundamental evils: the evil of greed, the evil of hatred, and the evil of delusion.
"The sixth set of three dharmas can be increased:
the absence of the root of greed, the absence of the root of hatred, and the absence of the root of delusion."
“Seventh, there are three qualities that are difficult to experience:
the sign of concentration, the sign of stillness, and the sign of arousal.
Eighth, there are three qualities that should be practiced.”
The three gates of liberation are emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
"The ninth set of three dharmas should be known:
the three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
“The thirteenth dharma: one’s own realized wisdom is beyond further training.
From the very beginning, as well as in future births, there is nothing therein that ought to be eliminated.

These constitute the thirty dharmas of the practitioner; they are not false, they are not otherwise; they are true and such as they are; they are unconfused and non-perverted. Such is the contemplation of the mind endowed with wisdom.”
"The first four dharmas: the practitioner ultimately becomes a wheel-turning monarch for gods and humans;
dwelling in a favorable district; relying on wise people; having self-uprightness and aspiration; and possessing roots from past lives."
"The second set of four dharmas for increasing practice:

the four foundations of mindfulness—contemplating the body, contemplating the body internally, and contemplating the body both internally and externally; not departing from mental awareness, fixing the mind, and abandoning worldly delusion and affliction."
"Sensation, mind, and phenomena are also to be contemplated in the same manner as the contemplation of the body.
"The third set of four dharmas should be known:
the four kinds of nutriment—edible food, contact-nutriment, volition-nutriment, and consciousness-nutriment."
"The fourth set of four dharmas should be abandoned:
the four taints—the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
"The fifth set of four dharmas should be diminished."
The four losses are: loss of precepts, loss of intention, loss of conduct, and loss of action.
"The sixth set of four dharmas consists of those that can be increased:
the four accomplishments, namely, accomplishment of precepts, accomplishment of intention, accomplishment of conduct, and accomplishment of action."
"The seventh set of four dharmas is difficult to know:
the Four Noble Truths—the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
"The eighth set of four dharmas brings about the possession of the four analytical insights."
The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, the knowledge of its cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
"The ninth set of four dharmas should be understood:

the four types of knowledge—limited knowledge, extensive knowledge, immeasurable and non-existent knowledge that is not to be known, and the knowledge that knows extensively and immeasurably yet is non-existent and not to be known."
"The fourteenth dharma is self-realization.
One should know: first, the Dharma-body; second, the Dharma-intent; third, the Dharma-eye; and fourth, the Dharma-wisdom."

These are the forty dharmas for the practitioner; they are not false, they are not otherwise; they are true and such as they are; they are unconfused and non-perverted; thus, with wisdom and mindfulness, one contemplates them as they truly are.
“The first five dharmas: the practitioner ultimately achieves the unconditioned through five kinds of mental abandonment.
What are these five?

The disciple of the Way possesses the faith of the Way and is firmly rooted in its foundation; none can destroy this. His forbearance is like that of a seer—whether it be a deva, a Māra, a Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
Furthermore, he is without concealment and without guile; his bodily conduct is truly upright and as it should be. His mind is fixed upon the wisdom of the Path, acting in accordance with it.
His body is free from much illness and remains in peace and well-being, maintaining his abdomen in a manner that is appropriate for his practice.

The body is neither excessively cold nor excessively hot; there is no time of anger, and it is harmonious, causing food and drink to be digested and consumed, making the body peaceful and well-regulated, and giving rise to the practice of energetic progress.

Possessing the skillful means of diligent application, one firmly attains the sublime Dharma; the mind does not abandon these skillful means, even at the cost of skin, sinews, bones, blood, and marrow. One exhausts all energy in diligent application without ceasing, for one must surely attain that which is to be practiced.
Regarding the practitioner who attains the Way through the wisdom that arises from the wisdom of origination and cessation: they must not grow weary of practice, but directly extinguish suffering.
These are the five kinds of mental abandonment.
"The second set of five dharmas is that which can increase the virtue of one's practice."
Regarding the five kinds of concentration:

when a disciple practicing the path maintains this body through self-mastery, they attain joy and happiness, which drenches and permeates their bodily conduct. Thus, throughout the entire body, there is not a single place that does not reach this joy and happiness arising from the bliss of self-mastery.
The one who bathes with wisdom is like a master of the wisdom-bath, and his disciples are likewise students of the wisdom-bath.
The disciples hold vessels, whether basins or cauldrons.

They soak the cleansing powder (kṣāra) in water; once soaked, they mix it so that the powder adheres to the grease. Because it has been soaked in the grease, the grease adheres both inside and out and does not disperse. This is due to having been soaked in the grease.

The practitioner of the path is also like this: this body, through self-guarding, gives rise to love and pleasure; it becomes moistened, harmonized, drawn near, and attached, such that there is nothing in the entire body that is not attached, arising from the joy of self-guarding.
"Disciples of the Way, these five kinds of concentration are the foremost practice.

There are also disciples of the Way whose bodies are already settled in joy and bliss, which drenches their bodily conduct. Throughout the body, there is not a single place that is not reached by this settled joy and bliss. It is like a spring at the head of a slope, a fountain or pool, which does not come from above, nor from the east, nor from the south, nor from the west, nor from the north; yet from the abundance of water in the spring, moisture arises and pervades the entire spring, drenching it so that there is not a single spot where the cool water does not reach."

When a disciple of the Way practices in this way, this body becomes settled in joy and happiness; it drenches the bodily formations until they pervade the entire body, reaching every part without exception, through that settled joy and happiness.
That a disciple of the Way possesses these five kinds of concentration is called the second practice.

Furthermore, there is a disciple of the Way whose body is not attached to craving or delight; even when connected with, reaching toward, drawing near to, or finding mutual approval with [objects], it does not experience joy or pleasure throughout the entire body.
For example, just as a lotus flower is born in water and grows in water—reaching from its roots to its stalks to its leaves—all of it is thoroughly drenched and saturated by cool water.
It is the same with the body of a disciple on the path: it is thoroughly drenched by the absence of craving and delight, such that the entire body is pervaded by this absence of craving and delight.
The disciple of the Way: these five kinds of concentration constitute the third practice.

Furthermore, there is the disciple of the Way whose body is purified by the mind; having already eliminated [defilements] through practice and perfected the practice, there is not a single place within the body that is not reached by the purification of the mind and the removal of mental [afflictions].

It is like the four castes and their sons; or like a white cotton cloth eight or nine zhang long, which completely wraps around a person’s head, feet, and body, leaving no part uncovered because of the purity of that white cotton cloth.

In this way, the disciple of the Way, having purified the body and removed [unwholesome] thoughts, continues in practice; there is no part of the entire body that has not reached the state of having covered and purified the mind and removed [unwholesome] thoughts.
"Disciples of the Way, these five kinds of concentration constitute the fourth practice.

Furthermore, there are disciples of the Way who, having received a body, contemplate the Truths; they have matured their mindfulness, matured their dwelling, and matured their reception, just as a standing person observes a sitting person, or a sitting person observes a reclining person."
When a disciple of the Way practices in this way, they receive and practice it with mental reflection until it is thoroughly mastered;
through thorough reception, thorough mindfulness, thorough application, and thorough reception—this fivefold concentration of the disciple of the Way constitutes the fifth practice.

"The third set of five dharmas should be known as fivefold: first, the aggregate of form; second, the aggregate of sensation; third, the aggregate of perception; fourth, the aggregate of formations; and fifth, the aggregate of consciousness."

"The fourth set of five dharmas: one should abandon the five hindrances—first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt."
"The fifth set of five things that should be diminished consists of the five mental spikes.

If a practitioner does not have faith in the Way, is doubtful, lacks resolve, and refuses to accept [the teachings], then this first mental spike remains unabandoned because they do not accept the instructions and admonitions of the Dharma."

It is also like this: when those who are still in training (śaikṣa) on the path—those renowned for their wisdom and those who are fellow students—direct harsh speech toward them, revile them, and exert themselves with intent malice to harass and invade them; and likewise when those who have attained the path—those renowned for their wisdom and those who are fellow students—are directed toward by harsh speech, reviled, and subjected to intent malice, harassment, and invasion. Such are the five mental spikes that have not yet been relinquished.
"The sixth set of five dharmas that should increase the Path consists of the five faculties:
first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of concentration; and fifth, the faculty of wisdom."
"The seventh set of five dharmas is difficult to receive.
One must practice the five factors to attain deliverance.

If a disciple of the Way receives the Way thoroughly, he does not dwell on sensual desire; his mind does not cling to desire, his mind does not find pleasure in desire, his mind does not rest in desire, and his mind does not transcend desire. His mind contracts, his mind becomes base, his mind does not arise, his mind is not employed, his mind is repelled, and his mind is defiled by not employing evil."
For example, just as chicken feathers or sinews shrink and wrinkle when placed in fire and cannot be stretched out again, so it is with the disciple who has seen the Path.

Their practice is firm and their mind does not dwell on sensual desire; they no longer employ sensual desire, they cannot be moved by sensual desire, and their mind does not fall into sensual desire. Thus the mind shrinks back; as the mind shrinks back, it does not arise [again], and they emerge from the thought of the Path.

Having already set out upon the practice, the mind arises and becomes firm; the mind emerges from non-mind and attains liberation. The mind does not contract, the mind does not become malicious, and the mind arises. The mind is without obstruction and has no further use; the mind is peaceful and secure because of its mental activity and its matured practice.

"Furthermore, if there arise from the causal conditions of craving further fetters, afflictions, and sorrows, one should reflect upon them as already being liberated from them, bringing them to rest, remaining unattached, and attaining detachment; thus, one will no longer undergo feelings arising from those causal conditions."
A practitioner such as this attains deliverance from desire, from anger and non-anger, from injury and non-injury, and from the material and the immaterial.

If a disciple of the Way maintains a firm mind and no longer dwells on the body—having maintained a firm mind and not dwelling on the body—he will have no desire for the body, no aversion toward the body, and no attachment to the body; his mind does not fall into craving, yet when evil thoughts arise, he remains undisturbed.
It is like the feathers and sinews of a chicken: when they enter the fire, they contract and shrivel, unable to be stretched out again.

A disciple of the Way is also like this; having seen the firm [truth], they no longer dwell upon the body. The mind does not identify with the body, the mind does not cling to the body, and the mind does not transcend itself. It contracts the mind so that evil thoughts do not arise; it maintains itself in stillness, ceasing what is evil, and remains non-active toward thoughts of the loathsome.

Desiring to cross over, one contemplates crossing over; the body becomes unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the mind encourages the mind, the mind finds satisfaction, the mind comes to rest, and the mind crosses over. The mind neither contracts nor recoils; the mind then extends its mindfulness so that there is nothing obstructing and nothing to be employed. The mind remains withdrawn and stilled, because it has become matured through the practice of conduct.

"If, due to bodily causes and conditions, sinful afflictions and distress arise; and having given rise to these sinful afflictions and distress, one attains liberation from them through cessation and non-attachment, then one will no longer experience further suffering due to those causes and conditions."
The disciple of the Way is thus: from the body, they attain the essential departure.

"The eighth fivefold dharma causes the Way to arise: the fivefold wisdom-concentration (*pañca-prajñā-samādhi*). For one who possesses the Way and virtue, there is nothing to which they are attached and nothing from which they follow; this is the first wisdom that arises within."
"This concentration is constant; it cannot be attained by ordinary people, but it can be attained by the wise.
Thus, two kinds of wisdom arise internally.
This concentration leads exclusively to the attainment of tranquility and the practice of the Path. Thus, three kinds of wisdom arise internally."
"This concentration is well-observed, leading to pleasant practice and its reception is also excellent; thus, four types of wisdom arise internally.
This concentration proceeds from this concentration, and one sits with mastery and rises with mastery; thus, five types of wisdom arise internally."

"Ninth, regarding the five dharmas, one should know the five stages of liberation: if a learner hears a discourse on the path from one who speaks of the path, or hears it from a person of wisdom, or hears it from a fellow student; having heard it as described, they understand the meaning of the Dharma; having understood the Dharma, they understand its meaning; having understood the meaning, they accept it; having accepted it, they rejoice; having rejoiced, their body becomes tranquil; and being tranquil, their mind becomes concentrated."

When the mind is concentrated, there is knowing as it is and seeing as it is; having known and seen thus, one then relinquishes them; having relinquished them, one does not cling; having no clinging, one attains liberation accordingly.
This is the practitioner’s single liberation: having practiced, one attains abiding;

having attained abiding, one attains right intention; having attained right intention, one attains concentration; having attained concentration, one attains the unraveling of fetters; having attained the unraveling of fetters, one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus reaches the unconditioned.
At times, even when the Buddha does not preach the sūtras, and his wise fellow-disciples likewise do not preach them, one simply recites them from memory exactly as they were heard and received.
This is the second liberation for the practitioner.

"Sometimes the Buddha does not preach the sutras, and his wise fellow-disciples likewise do not preach the sutras; rather, they fully explain the teachings to those who study them, exactly as they have heard the Dharma and received the Dharma."
This is the practitioner’s third liberation.

At times, when the Buddha does not preach the sūtras, the student merely reflects and contemplates alone in a secluded place according to what has been heard and received, or recites fully according to what has been heard and received; thus he attains understanding as it corresponds to reality and understands according to the Dharma—this is the practitioner’s fourth liberation.

"At times, it may not be exactly as heard or as received, nor is it even brought to mind; yet, through practice, one attains mastery over the fixed sign, mastery over reception, and mastery over mindfulness. Having practiced, one attains mastery over the fixed sign, mastery over reception, mastery over mindfulness, and mastery over practice. Accordingly, in accordance with the Dharma, one understands as it truly is and understands in accordance with the Dharma."

When one has understood as it should be understood, and has understood according to the Dharma, then birth arises; when birth has arisen, then compassion arises; when compassion has arisen, then there is bodily happiness, and through that bodily happiness, one knows happiness within the mind; once the mind is happy, it becomes stilled; then, through such knowledge and vision, remorse arises; with remorse, there is no further desire; with the absence of desire, one attains liberation—this is the practitioner’s fivefold liberation.

If a practitioner of the path attains this tranquility and attains this practice, their mind that has not yet attained tranquility shall attain it; their mind that has not yet become settled shall become settled; their fetters that have not yet been exhausted shall be exhausted; and they who have not yet attained the unconditioned transcendence of the world shall attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world.

"The fifteenth dharma to be personally realized is: first, not training in the aggregates; second, not training in the precepts; third, not training in meditative concentration; fourth, not training in wisdom; and fifth, not training in the liberation that transcends the world."

These fifty qualities of a trainee are not false, not otherwise, true, such as they are, unconfused, and unerring; they are to be contemplated by one possessing wisdom and mindfulness according to reality.
"The first of the six dharmas is the ultimate unconditioned state.

Not grasping at what is heavy in common with others, one’s bodily conduct is equal to that of those who abide in the Buddha-wisdom and study the same teachings; this dharma is not grasped as heavy by others. From this, one gains affection and from this, one gains respect. Having gained affection and having gained respect, one acts accordingly. One gathers together without dispute, practices concentration single-mindedly to achieve patience, and maintains equality in speech and equality in mental conduct. As for all precepts and practices, one does not violate them, does not breach them, does not slacken them, does not conceal them, and does not lose them."

For one who possesses the path, it is possible to practice fully; those who practice such precepts as I do should associate with those who possess wisdom and study together. Regarding the essential path sought through disenchantment, one should simply practice straightforwardly to extinguish suffering. Such people as these, and I likewise, should associate with those who possess wisdom and study together. This Dharma is not to be grasped or held as a secret treasure; furthermore, whatever beneficial qualities are attained through the Dharma, all that which is gained remains within the vessel [of the community]. Such benefits should be shared with fellow students, never kept hidden or withheld by oneself—this Dharma is not to be grasped or held as a secret treasure.

Because of this craving, one obtains respect and what is pleasing; having obtained craving, having obtained respect, and having obtained what is pleasing, one obtains conduct, obtains union, and obtains association, remaining without dispute or contention.
Practicing concentration with a single mind, one thereby attains patience.

"The second set of six dharmas is to guard the conduct of the six modes of cohabitation: when the eye sees forms, one neither rejoices nor feels aversion, but observes the mental formations with right knowledge."
Regarding the contemplation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and phenomena, one neither rejoices nor feels aversion; one simply contemplates the cessation of the mind without forgetting.
"The third set of six dharmas can be known thus."
The six internal sense bases (*āyatana*): the internal eye base, and the internal bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"The fourth set of six dharmas should be abandoned:
the six cravings (*tṛṣṇā*), namely craving for contact through the eye, and craving for contact through the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
"The fifth set of six things that may be diminished consists of the six forms of disrespect:

first, disrespect for the Buddha; second, disrespect for the Dharma; third, disrespect for one's fellow practitioners; fourth, disrespect for the precepts; fifth, harsh speech; and sixth, evil companions."
"The sixth set of six dharmas can be increased.

There are six forms of reverence: first, reverence for the Buddha; second, reverence for the Dharma; third, reverence for one's fellow practitioners; fourth, reverence for the precepts; fifth, pleasant speech; and sixth, virtuous friends."
"The seventh of the six things that are difficult to receive:
there are six practices for transcending the world.
If someone says, 'I possess a mind of equanimity and concentration; I have already practiced and already attained it.'"
If he further says,
"The anger within my mind has not yet been resolved," you may reply:
"Do not speak thus.
Why? Because such a thing does not exist."
Having already attained equanimity of mind and concentration, having already practiced, already acted, and already possessed [this state], how could there be anger?
Such a thing is impossible. Why is this so?
"There is the concentration of equanimity, for the purpose of removing ill-will.
Second, if a practitioner says:
"I possess the concentrated mind of loving-kindness; it has been cultivated, practiced, and established within me, yet the intent to kill remains and is not removed."
One should reply:
"It is not as you say. Why is that?"

If one has already attained the concentration of a mind of loving-kindness, and has already practiced, performed, and possessed it, could there possibly be an intention to kill? There is not. Why is this so?
"Having already attained the meditative concentration of a benevolent mind, one is free from any intent to kill.
Third, for the sake of those who are still training, he says:
"I possess a mind of joy and meditative equanimity; these have been practiced, performed, and attained. Yet, if my mind does not come to rest, it is not sufficient."
He replied, "Do not speak thus.
For what reason?
It is not possible that one who has already attained equanimity, concentration, and a settled mind—who has practiced, increased, and mastered them—should not be concentrated or unable [to remain so].
Why is this? It is not possible.
For what reason?
"Equanimity of mind is for the purpose of removing what is not fixed.
Fourth, if a learner says:
"I possess the meditative mind of contemplation; it has been practiced, performed, and attained by me, yet craving and ill-will have not been eliminated."
One should reply:
"Do not speak thus. Why is this?"
"Once one possesses the mind of meditative concentration through contemplation, there will be no more craving, desire, or ill-will.
Fifth, the practitioner says:
"I have no doubt; it is simply that my mind is incapable."
One should reply:
"Do not speak thus.
For what reason?
"Because one understands the essentials and is free from doubt.
Sixth, for the practitioner, it is said:
"Having already attained sufficient concentration of mind, one simply directs the mind toward mindfulness and cognition."
One should reply: "It is not as you say;
such a thing does not exist. Furthermore, one should not entertain the thought that one has attained concentration.
Once the mind is free from all thoughts, it is sufficient; to again engage the mind in the activity of thinking and perceiving—such a thing does not exist."
Why is this? One whose mind has already attained liberation should not engage in further recollection.

"The eighth set of six dharmas consists of ensuring that one possesses the six recollections: first, recollection of the Buddha; second, recollection of the Dharma; third, recollection of fellow practitioners; fourth, recollection of the precepts; fifth, recollection of generosity; and sixth, recollection of the devas."
"Ninth, there are six dharmas that should be known.

There are six immeasurables: first, the immeasurable of vision; second, the immeasurable of hearing; third, the immeasurable of gain; fourth, the immeasurable of precepts; fifth, the immeasurable of service; and sixth, the immeasurable of mindfulness."
"The sixteenth factor is the realization through personal knowledge.

There are six knowledges: first, the power of psychic transformation; second, clairaudience; third, knowledge of the minds of others; fourth, knowledge of past lives; fifth, knowledge of rebirth in future states; and sixth, knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters."

These sixty dharmas of the practitioner are not otherwise, not different; they are true and such as they are, unconfused and non-perverted; they are observed by one possessing wisdom and mindfulness according to reality.
"The first seven dharmas lead the practitioner ultimately to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The seven treasures are: first, the treasure of faith; second, the treasure of ethical discipline; third, the treasure of moral dread (*apatrāpya*); fourth, the treasure of shame (*hrī*); fifth, the treasure of learning; sixth, the treasure of generosity; and seventh, the treasure of wisdom."
"The second set of seven dharmas that should be practiced consists of the seven factors of enlightenment:

first, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; second, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena; third, the factor of enlightenment of energy; fourth, the factor of enlightenment of joy; fifth, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration; and seventh, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
“The third set of seven dharmas should be known:

the seven existences—first, the existence of non-existence; second, the existence of animals; third, the existence of hungry ghosts; fourth, the existence of humans; fifth, the existence of devas; sixth, the existence of becoming; and seventh, the intermediate existence.”
“The fourth set of seven things to be abandoned consists of the seven fetters:

first, the fetter of sensual desire; second, the fetter of ill will; third, the fetter of attachment to existence; fourth, the fetter of self-conceit; fifth, the fetter of wrong views; sixth, the fetter of ignorance; and seventh, the fetter of doubt.”
"The fifth set of seven dharmas that should be diminished consists of the seven dharmas of the evil person:

first, lack of faith; second, lack of moral dread (*apatrāpya*); third, lack of shame (*hrī*); fourth, lack of diligence; fifth, loss of mindfulness; sixth, lack of concentration; and seventh, lack of wisdom."
"The sixth and seventh [sets of] seven dharmas increase wisdom.

The seven dharmas that constitute wisdom are: first, faith; second, a sense of shame (*hrī*); third, a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); fourth, the arousal of diligence; fifth, guarding the mind; sixth, concentration; and seventh, wisdom."
"The seventh set of seven dharmas is difficult to comprehend.
There are seven stations of consciousness where the body is material and distinct from the [mental] body, and possesses distinct characteristics.
For example, among humans or among devas; this is the first station of consciousness."
“There are those with material form who have diverse bodies and a single perception, such as the devas in heaven known as the Brahmās who dwell above; this is the second station of consciousness.”
“There is a sphere of form where there is a single body and a single perception;
for example, the devas named Ābhāsvara—this is the third station of consciousness.
There is a sphere of form where practitioners dwell, having entirely transcended form and extinguished ill-will, dwelling in immeasurable conduct.”
For example, the heavens are named "empty," which serves as the dwelling place for the four consciousnesses.
When there is a practitioner who dwells in the sphere of formless existence, they all attain liberation through emptiness, and their practice of consciousness comes to rest in the immeasurable.
For example, there is a heaven named Vijñāna; this is the place where the five consciousnesses abide.
Therein exists that which does not dwell in form or action, having neither perception nor being devoid of perception.
For example, there is a heaven named "Non-perception," which is the abode of the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the eighth set of seven dharmas, practice them so as to bring about a concentrated mind:
first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; and seventh, right concentration.
"Ninth, there are seven things that should be known.

There are seven ways of manifesting gratitude: first, for one who practices the path, the intention is set upon the Buddha, faith enters, and the roots of the path arise; thus abiding, nothing can destroy them—not a śramaṇa, nor a brāhmaṇa, nor a deva, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor any other wanderer in the world."

Second, it is for upholding the precepts, guarding the discipline, and encompassing the moral code; it involves entering and exiting with the dread of the penalty of death, maintaining the precepts, and training in the rules of conduct.
Third, it is for having good spiritual friends, having good companions in residence, and having a good refuge.
Fourth is dwelling alone without a companion, practicing with focused application of body and mind.
Fifth is maintaining the practice of vigor and firm diligence, never abandoning the skillful means of the Dharma.
Sixth is the mental resolve: "Even if my body, skin, muscles, bones, blood, and vital organs should perish, I must exert diligence in whatever is to be practiced.

Seventh is being one who has a protector, who practices with steadfastness, and who does not abandon skillful means; having attained what is to be attained through the practice of the Dharma, one does not cease one's diligence before reaching it, guarding the practice of the mind, maintaining the supreme holding of the mind, practicing for a long time, and speaking for a long time so that the mind does not forget.
Seventh is the mindfulness of wisdom and conduct, which realizes arising and ceasing and attains the mind of wisdom.
This is the seventh manifest grace.
"The seventeenth dharma should be realized."

First, the existence of the Dharma; second, the possession of understanding; third, knowledge of the proper time; fourth, knowledge of contentment; fifth, knowledge of oneself; sixth, knowledge of the assembly; seventh, knowledge of the past and future of individuals.

These seventy dharmas of the practitioner are not false, not different, and possess truth and suchness; they are non-delusive and non-perverted, being observed by one who maintains wisdom and mental attention according to reality.

The Dīrgha Āgama: The Sūtra on the Tenfold Law of Retribution, Volume One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. "First, there are eight dharmas by which a practitioner increases their fundamental practice; these are the eight causes and conditions for attaining the dharma of wisdom."
What are the eight?

First, if a practitioner relies on the instructions they have received and also relies on wise companions in the training, this is the fundamental practice; by means of it, one who has not yet attained wisdom shall attain wisdom.
This is the causal condition for the first dharma.

Having relied upon the Buddha and other wise companions in the training, one obtains from time to time the hearing of subtle Dharma sutras; this increases one's fundamental practice, so that if one has not yet attained fundamental wisdom, one shall attain it.
These are the causes and conditions for these two dharmas.
"Having heard the Dharma, one withdraws the body and withdraws the mind; through the causal conditions of this fundamental practice, one who has not yet attained wisdom shall attain wisdom."
These are the causes and conditions for the three dharmas.
Having heard the Dharma, one practices with diligence; from this, one increases one's fundamental practice and attains wisdom where it was previously unattained.
These are the causes and conditions for the four dharmas.

"Exerting all one's strength to guard the practice of mindfulness, practicing for a long time and speaking for a long time, desiring to attain what is to be attained through mindfulness—this is the increase of practice; that which was not yet attained wisdom is now attained.
These are the five causal conditions."
"Receiving instruction on the Dharma is like practicing the Dharma; it is an increase in practice, whereby one who has not attained wisdom shall attain it.
These are the six causal conditions.
Delighting in the Dharma and delighting in its practice, and frequently reciting the sutras, is an increase in practice, whereby one who has not attained wisdom shall attain it."
These are the causal conditions for the seven dharmas.

"To know the increase and decrease of the five aggregates and their modes of activity: whether it be form, the origin of form, or the cessation of form; and likewise feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—whether it be the arising of consciousness, the transcendence of consciousness, or the increase of fundamental practice through which one who has not yet attained wisdom attains wisdom."
These are the causal conditions for the eight dharmas.
"The second set of eight dharmas consists of those practices by which one attains the Way.

These are the Eightfold Path: first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration."
"The third set of eight dharmas: one should know the eight worldly dharmas—first, gain; second, loss; third, fame; fourth, infamy; fifth, censure; sixth, praise; seventh, pleasure; and eighth, pain."
"The fourth set of eight dharmas should be abandoned:

first, lack of rectitude in view; second, lack of rectitude in thought; third, lack of rectitude in speech; fourth, lack of rectitude in dharma; fifth, lack of rectitude in action; sixth, lack of rectitude in means; seventh, lack of rectitude in intention; eighth, lack of rectitude in concentration."
"The fifth set of eight factors that may be diminished consists of the eight kinds of indolence that obstruct the path of diligence.

Suppose a practitioner is in a commandery, a district, a village, or elsewhere, and having relied upon his practice, rises at dawn, puts on his robes, takes up his alms-bowl, and enters the commandery or district to seek food."
He thought to himself,
"I shall obtain much food to my liking. Having set out,
he did not obtain much food to his liking, and so he reflected:
"Today I am unable to eat as much as I desire; my body is so weak that I cannot sit, so I shall lie down and remain lying down.

Thus, he no longer seeks the means for transcending the world, nor does he strive for what has not yet been attained, nor seek liberation for what has not yet been understood, nor seek self-knowledge for what he has not yet known.
This is the first kind of dull-wittedness, a path of non-diligence.

"If a practitioner is in a commandery, a district, or a village, or practices in dependence on other places, they rise at dawn, put on their robes, take up the alms bowl, and enter the commandery or district to seek food."
He thinks to himself:
"I shall eat much food that is to my liking.
Having obtained much food that is to his liking, he thinks to himself:
"I have eaten much edible food this morning," he thought to himself.
"Because I have eaten so much edible food this morning, my body is heavy; I am unable to walk or sit, and it causes me to lie prostrate."
He then lay down.

Lacking the skillful means to transcend the world, he failed to attain what he ought to have attained; he failed to realize what he ought to have realized; and he failed to know by himself that which he ought to have known for himself.
These are the two kinds of delusion.
"Furthermore, there may be a time when a practitioner, or when it is time for him to go out and practice the Way, a thought arises in his mind:
'It is my duty to go out and practice the Way, yet I am unable to go out and practice the Way; I am unable to receive instruction and practice accordingly, so let me lie down and rest.'"

No longer seeking the means for transcending the world, they fail to attain what has not yet been attained, fail to understand what has not yet been understood, and fail to realize what has not yet been realized.
These are the three kinds of delusion.
"Sometimes a practitioner walks the path during the day and thinks to himself:
'Having walked the path since morning, my body is weary and I am unable to sit and practice; let me lie down and rest.'"
He then lay down prostrate.

Lacking the skillful means to transcend the world, he would either attain what should be attained or fail to attain it; he would either understand what should be understood or fail to understand it; he would either realize and witness for himself what should be realized and witnessed, or fail to realize and witness it for himself.
These are the four kinds of dullness.
"At times, when a practitioner ought to practice well, they think:
'I ought to practice well, yet I am unable to practice; I cannot receive and uphold the instructions and admonitions; let me lie down for a moment.'"
He then lay down prostrate;

he did not seek the means for transcending the world. That which he ought to have attained, he failed to attain; that which he ought to have understood, he failed to understand; that which he ought to have realized through personal knowledge, he failed to realize through personal knowledge.
These are the five kinds of dullness.
"At times, the practitioner thinks:
'I have practiced the Path this morning; my body is so weak that I cannot sit, so let me lie down.'"

Having already lain down in defeat, he does not seek the means for transcending the world; what should be attained, he does not attain; what should be understood, he does not understand; and what should be personally realized through direct knowledge, he does not realize.
These are the six kinds of delusion.
At times, when a practitioner has fallen ill and suffers, he thinks:
"I have already been afflicted by suffering; my body is so weak that I cannot walk or sit, and I must lie prostrate."

He then lay down prostrate; lacking the skillful means to transcend the world, he would neither attain what could be attained, nor understand what could be understood, nor realize through his own knowledge what could be realized through his own knowledge.
These are the seven kinds of dullness.
"At times, a practitioner has just recovered from illness and, not long after, thinks:
'I have just recovered from illness; my body is so weak that I cannot walk or sit, so let me lie down.'"

He then lay down prostrate, seeking no means for transcending the world; whether he should attain or not attain, whether he should understand or not understand, whether he should personally realize and witness it or not personally realize and witness it.
These are the eight types of dullness.
"The sixth set of eight dharmas is the path of increasing practice, the path of the eightfold application of diligence.

As for the practitioner: whether in a commandery, a district, a village, or any other place where they rely on their practice, they rise at dawn, put on their robes, take up their alms bowl, and enter the commandery or district to seek food."
He thought to himself,
"I shall obtain much food to eat.
Not obtaining much food to eat, he thought to himself again:
"I must not eat too much; by keeping my body light, I shall be able to move and sit, which will enable me to practice skillful means.
Thus, he brings what has not been attained to attainment, what has not been understood to understanding, and what has not been self-realized to self-realization.
This is the first skillful means of diligence.
"At times, when a practitioner is in a commandery,
a district, or a village, or practicing in dependence on other locations, he rises at dawn, puts on his robes, takes up his alms bowl, and enters the commandery or district to seek food."
He thought to himself,
"I shall obtain much food to eat.
Having obtained much food to eat, he then reflected:
"Having already received much food fit for consumption this morning, my body possesses the strength to sit and walk forward; let me therefore seek skillful means.
What has not yet been attained shall be attained; what has not yet been understood shall be understood; what has not yet been self-realized shall be self-realized."
These are the two skillful means of diligence.
"At times, when a practitioner intends to go out, the thought arises:
'I ought to go out, yet my body cannot move, nor can I receive instructions on how to proceed; let me give orders and seek a skillful means.'"
"To apply skillful means for one's own path so as to attain what has not yet been attained, to realize what has not yet been realized, and to achieve self-knowledge where there was previously none—
these are the three skillful means of diligence."
"At times, while practicing, a practitioner gives rise to this thought:

'I have already been practicing the Path for some time, yet I am unable to practice the Path myself, nor can I respectfully attend to the instructions and admonitions that would cause me to disclose my transgressions.'"

To employ skillful means so that what has not been attained shall be attained, what has not been understood shall be understood, and what has not been personally realized shall be personally realized—these are the four applications of diligence.
"At times, a practitioner who is practicing may think:
'I am unable to carry out the practice and accomplish the teaching; perhaps someone else should go before me to seek the skillful means.

Thereupon, they proceed with the skillful means: what has not yet been attained shall be attained, what has not yet been understood shall be understood, and what has not yet been personally realized shall be personally realized."
These are the five skillful means of diligence.
At times, a practitioner, having completed the practice, reflects:
"I have already completed the practice and can no longer perform it further; I shall fulfill the instructions so that I may close off what has been transgressed."

He then seeks skillful means regarding what has been transgressed and closed off: that which was not yet attained he shall attain; that which was not yet understood he shall understand; and that which was not yet self-realized he shall realize for himself.
These are the six skillful means of diligence.
"Sometimes, when a practitioner suffers from extreme physical illness, they think:
'I am suffering from extreme illness; it may be that I will die from this at any time. I must seek to practice skillful means for even a brief moment.'"
"What has not yet been attained shall be attained; what has not yet been understood shall be understood; what has not yet been personally realized shall be personally realized.
This is the seventh application of diligence.
"Furthermore, at times, a practitioner who has recently recovered from illness may think:"
"Having just recently arisen from illness, I fear that the illness may return; therefore, I shall now stand before it and seek skillful means.
Thus, he stood before it and sought skillful means, until what was not yet attained was attained, what was not yet understood was understood, and what was not yet self-realized was self-realized.
These are the eight skillful means of diligence.
"The seventh of the eight dharmas is difficult to receive:
the eight liberations."

At times, a practitioner, internally perceiving form, externally perceives forms—whether few, beautiful, or ugly—knowing those forms at will and seeing them at will, with mental perception likewise being as it is; this is the first liberation.
"Sometimes a practitioner contemplates forms internally while seeing forms externally; this is the second liberation.
Sometimes a practitioner dwells in the perception of pure liberation, experiencing it with the body; this is the third liberation."
"Transcending all form, with the cessation of ill will, and being without various perceptions or non-perceptions, one dwells in the attainment of emptiness; this is the fourth liberation.

Transcending all emptiness, one dwells in the attainment of the perception of consciousness; transcending all consciousness, one dwells in the attainment of the sphere of nothingness; this is the fifth liberation."
"All things transcend non-existence; one does not employ the perception of non-existence, nor the practice of the perception of non-existence—this is the sixth liberation.
All things transcend the perception of existence and do not practice the perception of non-existence—this is the seventh liberation."
“The cessation of perception, the body’s knowledge of sensation, and the practice—these are the eight liberations.
Regarding the eighth set of eight dharmas, there are altogether eight recollections of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa-anusmṛti*). What are these eight?”
"First, the Dharma of the Path is for those with few desires, not for those with many desires.
Second, the Dharma of the Path is for those who are content;
for those who are discontented, there is no Dharma of the Path."
"Third, there are the dharmas of the path for those who practice and receive them;
for those who do not practice and receive them, there are no dharmas of the path.
Fourth, there are the dharmas of the path for those who are diligent."
For those who lack diligence, there is no path or Dharma.
There are five factors of the path for one who guards the mind;
for one who does not guard the mind, there is no path or Dharma.
"Six are the factors of the path for one whose mind is concentrated;
for one whose mind is not concentrated, there are no factors of the path.
Seven are the factors of the path for one who possesses wisdom."
Those who lack wisdom do not possess the Dharma of the Path.
"The eightfold path is the Dharma of the Path; there is no pleasure in the household life, nor is there any lack of pleasure in the household life.
To dwell together brings the pleasure of the household, but to dwell together does not bring the Dharma of the Path."
These are the eight recollections of a great person.
"The ninth set of eight dharmas: one should know these eight dharmas. What are they?
One perceives forms internally and sees forms externally—whether few, beautiful, or ugly—and attains mastery over those forms, knowing oneself to be masterful and seeing with mastery."
The mental application of attention is the first mastery.
Internally attending to forms while externally seeing forms, one sees forms without being overwhelmed by them; thus, in one's practice, there is mastery of knowledge and mastery of vision.
Such a perception is the second mastery.
"Having no perception of internal forms, one sees external forms as few—whether beautiful or ugly—and regarding those forms that exist, one knows them at will and sees them at will."
Such a perception is the third mastery.

Not attending to forms internally, one sees forms externally—whether they be beautiful or ugly; wherever forms exist, one knows them with mastery and sees them with mastery regarding their range of activity.
Such a perception is the fourth mastery.
Internally perceiving the notion of form, one externally sees forms that are blue—blue in color, blue in luster, and blue in appearance.

Just as a flower named *utpala* is blue in color, blue in luster, and blue in appearance, so too, internally perceiving the notion of form, one externally sees forms that are blue—blue in color, blue in luster, and blue in appearance.
Such a perception is the fifth mastery:
"Internally perceiving the notion of form, one externally sees forms that are yellow—yellow in color, yellow in luster, and appearing as yellow.

Just as, for example, a *kaṇikāra* flower, or a garment of the most brilliant yellow color, is yellow in color, yellow in luster, and appears as yellow; in the same way, internally perceiving the notion of form, one externally sees forms that are yellow—yellow in color, yellow in luster, and appearing as yellow."
Such a perception is the sixth mastery:
"Having the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms as red—red in color, red in luster, and red in appearance.
It is like a safflower, or like a crimson robe that is red in color, red in luster, and red in appearance."

In this way, the practitioner, having the perception of internal forms, sees external forms as red—red in color, red in luster, and red in appearance; such forms being present, he knows them with mastery and sees them with mastery.
Such a perception is the seventh mastery.
Having the perception of internal form, one sees external forms as white—white in color, with a white luster, and clearly seen as white.
It is like a bright star, or like a perfectly refined white cloth that is white in color, with a white luster, and clearly seen as white.

Thus, the practitioner, having the perception of internal form, sees external forms as white—white in color, white in appearance, and clearly seen; such being the case with these forms, they know them with mastery and see them with mastery.
Having such a perception is the eighth mastery.
"This is the eighteenth dharma:
knowing at the time when one should know for oneself; this is the power of one who practices the eightfold absence of attachment."

The practitioner who is free from attachment views sensual desire as being like fire; thus he knows it and thus he perceives it. He causes thoughts of sensual desire to pass away and ensures that his wisdom and mind no longer cling to them. This non-clinging is the first power.
“When the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness is perfected and one is without attachment, this constitutes the second power.
When the practice of the four right efforts is perfected, this constitutes the third power.”
"When the practice of the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda) is fully perfected, these constitute the four powers.
When the practice of the five faculties (indriya) is fully perfected, these constitute the five powers.
When the practice of the five powers is fully perfected, these constitute the six powers."
"When the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment is fulfilled, these constitute the seven powers.
When the practice of the eightfold path is fulfilled, these constitute the eight powers.
These are the eighty dharmas for the practitioner."
This is neither wrong nor different; it possesses truth and suchness, and is without delusion or inversion. This is how one who possesses wisdom observes with the mind:
"Of the first nine dharmas, the practitioner frequently practices the nine mental states of joy."
What are the nine? First is the joy of hearing the Dharma;

second is the joy of mindfulness; third is the joy of joy; fourth is the joy of bliss; fifth is the joy of the pliancy of feeling; sixth is the joy of tranquility; seventh is the joy of concentration; eighth is the joy of cessation; ninth is the joy of detachment.
“The second set of nine dharmas consists of attaining purity through diligence. What are the nine? First, attaining purity through the perfection of diligence;

second, attaining purity through the perfection of the mind; third, attaining purity through the perfection of views; fourth, attaining purity through the perfection of overcoming doubt; fifth, attaining purity through the perfection of the path; sixth, attaining purity through the vision of wisdom as it truly is; seventh, attaining purity through the perfection of severing craving for views and wisdom; eighth, the eradication of the seeds [of existence]; and ninth, transcendence of the world.”
"The third set of nine dharmas: one should know the nine abodes of beings. What are the nine?
There are beings with form who are diverse in body and diverse in perception."
The human realm is one abode of devas;
this is the first station of devas.
There is a station of devas with form, possessing diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the devas called Brahmā, who have attained the highest state of mental life.
These are the two abodes of the divine.
There is an abode of the divine with form, where there is a single body but manifold perceptions, such as the heaven named Abhasvara (Radiant).
This is the third abode of the divine.
“There is a station of divine abiding with form, wherein there is a single body and a single perception, such as the heaven named Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
This is the fourth station of divine abiding.
There is a station of divine abiding with form, wherein one neither perceives nor perceives again, such as the heaven named Non-perception (*Asaṃjñin*).”
These are the five abodes of the deities of clarity.

There is an abode of the deities of formlessness wherein one transcends all form and extinguishes ill-will; it is not that one does not attend to it, but rather one practices the perception of infinite space within a manifold body, like the heaven named Ākāśānantyāyatana (the Sphere of Infinite Space).
These are the six abodes of the divine mind.

There is an abode of the formless mind that completely transcends all space, wherein there is the immeasurable consciousness, wisdom, conduct, and mental abiding; this is comparable to the heaven named Ābhāsvara (the Heaven of Radiant Consciousness).
These are the seven stations of consciousness.

There is a station of consciousness that does not abide in form, wherein one completely transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness through the wisdom of nothingness, and practices the realization of the sphere of nothingness; it is like the heaven named the Sphere of Nothingness.
These are the eight bases of divine abiding (*brahmavihāra*).

There is a base of divine abiding where there is neither perception nor non-perception; it is the ultimate transcendence through wisdom regarding all that is free from desire, wherein there is no perception and yet one does not depart from perception, reaching the final cessation. It is, for example, like the heaven named Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
These are the nine abodes of the divine mind.
"The fourth set of nine dharmas:
one should uproot the nine fetters."
What are the nine? Sensual desire is the first fetter;

ill will is the second fetter; conceit is the third fetter; delusion is the fourth fetter; wrong view is the fifth fetter; doubt is the sixth fetter; greed is the seventh fetter; envy is the eighth fetter; and stinginess is the ninth fetter.
"The fifth set of nine dharmas:
one should extinguish the nine roots of resentment. What are these nine? "

If a practitioner intends to bestow evil, intends to cause distress, or intends to inflict injury, and furthermore contemplates other evils—if the practitioner directs his thoughts toward these things and affliction arises therefrom, this constitutes the first affliction.

"If a practitioner has already committed an evil deed, has already bestowed harm, has already caused distress, has already committed an invasion, or has already bestowed other evils—if the practitioner reflects upon these things and, from this, gives rise to vexation, this constitutes the second vexation."

"If a practitioner later wishes to inflict harm, wishes to cause unease, wishes to inflict injury, or wishes to inflict other evils upon another, and if that practitioner directs their thoughts toward this, affliction arises from it."
These are the three vexations.

"If a practitioner has a close friend, and that friend wishes to do harm to him—wishing to inflict evil, wishing to inflict insecurity, wishing to inflict injury, or wishing to inflict other evils—if the practitioner dwells upon this thought, vexation arises from it once again; these are the four vexations."

“If a practitioner has a relative or close friend who has already given them what is harmful, what is distressing, what is injurious, or other such evils, and if the practitioner dwells upon this, and from this a vexation arises, these are the five vexations.”

"If a practitioner has someone toward whom he feels affection and intimacy, yet later that person wishes to treat the practitioner with hostility, wishes to cause him unease, wishes to inflict injury, or wishes to subject him to other evils—if the practitioner reflects upon this, and from it arises vexation, this constitutes the sixth form of malice."

"If a practitioner has fears that are unfavorable, or if someone assists the practitioner who has such fears—desiring to bestow peace, desiring to resolve the encroachment, and not wishing for any further evil—if the practitioner then thinks, 'This is not acceptable,' and from this gives rise to vexation, these are the seven vexations."

"If a practitioner has fears that are unfavorable, or if there are those who wish to assist the practitioner but find it unfavorable; if [the practitioner] has already bestowed peace, already resolved an offense, and does not wish for further evil, yet the practitioner turns toward thoughts that this [assistance] should not arise, and from this gives rise to vexation—these are the eight vexations."

"If a practitioner has fears that are unfavorable, or if others have fears for the practitioner that are unfavorable, and having already assisted, comforted, or liberated them from such encroachments and other evils, the practitioner nevertheless harbors thoughts of resentment toward them; wishing to cause those who were unfavorable to become comfortable, he gives rise to vexation from this—this is the ninth ground for vexation."
"The ninth set of six dharmas:
one should contemplate the removal of the nine mental afflictions.
What are the nine? "

Or at times, a practitioner thinks: "This person causes me to perish, causes me to fall into another state, deprives me of happiness, and makes me insecure; they have already done me harm. Holding such a mind of malice and resentment toward them, if the practitioner directs their thoughts toward this, this constitutes the first [basis of resentment].

"Furthermore, there may be a practitioner who thinks: 'This person causes me to perish, causes me to have others, causes me to lack happiness, and causes me to be insecure; they see and act toward me with malice. If the practitioner harbors such a mind of ill-will and resentment toward them, this constitutes the second [obstacle].

"Furthermore, when a practitioner thinks: 'This person causes my ruin, causes me to have others [as enemies], causes me to lack happiness, and causes me to be insecure; they will surely do me harm. Holding such a mind of malice and resentment toward that practitioner—if one dwells upon this thought, this constitutes the third [type of ill will]."

"Furthermore, there are times when a practitioner has someone toward whom they feel such thoughts as: 'This person who is dear and close to me—may they perish, may they fall into the power of others, may they be deprived of happiness, and may they be unsettled. Having already committed an evil act against them, they maintain this malicious and vexed intention. If the practitioner directs their mindfulness toward such a person, this constitutes the fourth [basis of resentment]."

"Furthermore, at times a practitioner may have someone toward whom they feel: 'This person is dear and close to me; I wish for them to perish, to fall into the hands of others, to be deprived of happiness, and to be unsettled. Because of this, they harbor ill will and direct their mind toward that person with such malicious intent. If a practitioner contemplates in this way, this constitutes the fifth [basis of resentment]."

"Furthermore, at times a practitioner may have someone toward whom this mind arises: 'I have a close friend whom I wish to cause to perish, to fall into the hands of others, to be deprived of happiness, and to be unsettled. Having committed such an evil act, he maintains this malicious and vexed intention. If the practitioner directs his mindfulness toward this, this constitutes the sixth [basis]."

"Or at times, when a practitioner has such a thought arise: 'This person is not favorable to me; I harbor thoughts of ill will toward them, thoughts of making them uneasy, and thoughts of making them inauspicious; may my enemy have benefit, peace, happiness, and security. Having formed and maintained this intent of malice, if the practitioner then directs his mind toward that person, this constitutes the seventh [thought]."

"Furthermore, there may be times when a practitioner harbors such thoughts: 'He is not one who is favorable toward me; he dwells on what is unwholesome for me, dwelling on what causes me unease, dwelling on what brings me misfortune; yet he wishes for my enemies to have profit, peace, happiness, and well-being. Seeing them acting thus and maintaining such a hostile intention, if the practitioner directs his mind toward this thought, these constitute the eight [grounds of resentment]."

"Furthermore, there may be a time when a practitioner has such a thought arise: 'This person is not favorable toward me; I harbor ill will toward them, wishing for their unease and misfortune, while I wish for my enemy to have profit, peace, happiness, and well-being. If the practitioner directs their mindfulness toward this, this constitutes the ninth [thought]."

"The seventh set of nine dharmas is difficult to receive. There are nine bases of dwelling. What are the nine? [1] Dwelling with a mind imbued with loving-kindness toward one direction, [2] toward a second direction, [3] toward a third direction, [4] toward a fourth direction, [5] above, [6] below, [7] across, [8] everywhere, and [9] in all respects, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. [The same is repeated for compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. These are the nine bases of dwelling. This is the seventh set of nine dharmas that is difficult to receive. What is the eighth set of nine dharmas that is difficult to receive? There are nine successive abidings. What are the nine? [1] One dwells having attained the first dhyāna; [2] one dwells having attained the second dhyāna; [3] one dwells having attained the third dhyāna; [4] one dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna; [5] one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space; [6] one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; [7] one dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness; [8] one dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; [9] one dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. These are the nine successive abidings. This is the eighth set of nine dharmas that is difficult to receive. What is the ninth set of nine dharmas that is difficult to receive? There are nine progressive meditative attainments. What are the nine? [1] One attains the first dhyāna, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the second dhyāna; [2] one attains the second dhyāna, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the third dhyāna; [3] one attains the third dhyāna, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna; [4] one attains the fourth dhyāna, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space; [5] one attains the sphere of infinite space, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; [6] one attains the sphere of infinite consciousness, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness; [7] one attains the sphere of nothingness, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; [8] one attains the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling; [9] one attains the cessation of perception and feeling, emerges from it, and dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
