If a practitioner attains faith as a basis for abiding and is able to abandon what is unwholesome while embracing what is wholesome, this is the first basis for abiding;
if a practitioner applies the mind to practice and abandons non-practice, this is the second basis for abiding;
if a practitioner arouses diligence and abandons the lack of diligence, this is the third basis for abiding.
If a practitioner dwells in solitude and maintains self-restraint, abandoning non-restraint, this constitutes the four reliances;
if a practitioner is able to endure these reliances and, having thus attained dwelling through reliance, achieves correct discernment, this constitutes the five reliances;
if a practitioner abandons one dharma, this constitutes the six reliances.
Having abandoned one dharma, one understands another dharma; this is the seventh station of reliance.
Having understood one dharma, one receives another dharma; this is the eighth station of reliance.
Having received one dharma, one practices another dharma; this is the ninth station of reliance.

“Eighth and ninth: the nine successive attainments of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. What are the nine? [1] One attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, having completely transcended sense-desire, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. [2] With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, one attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is inner serenity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. [3] With the fading away of rapture, one dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly aware; experiencing pleasure with the body, one attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as ‘dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and pleasure. [4] With the abandoning of both pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, one attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, purified by equanimity and mindfulness. [5] By completely transcending forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. [6] By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. [7] By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ one attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. [8] By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, one attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. [9] By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.”
Establishing mindfulness in the first dhyāna constitutes the first concentration;
proceeding from the first to the second dhyāna constitutes the second concentration;
proceeding from the second to the third dhyāna constitutes the third concentration.
From the completion of the third and fourth *dhyānas*, there are four concentrations;
from the completion of the fourth *dhyāna* to the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), there are five concentrations;
from the completion of emptiness to the transcendence of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*), there are six concentrations.
From the completion of consciousness, one successively transcends the absence of desire; this constitutes the seventh absorption.
From the completion of the absence of desire, one successively transcends the absence of perception; this constitutes the eighth absorption.
From the completion of the absence of perception, one successively transcends cessation; this constitutes the ninth absorption.
"The ninety-ninth teaching:
one should know that there are nine improper times when a person cannot practice, and during which the ninth practice remains incomplete.
What are these nine?
"First, there may be times when a person is in hell; as long as their retribution is not yet exhausted, they shall not be permitted to attain the Way.
Second, there may be times when one is among the animals; as long as their retribution is not yet exhausted, they shall not be permitted to attain the Way."
"Third, sometimes they are among the hungry ghosts; as long as their retribution for past offenses is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to attain the Way.
Fourth, sometimes they are among the long-lived devas; as long as their merit is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to attain the Way."

"First, there may be times when one is in a place where the Dharma and its meaning are unknown; since there is no one to explain them, one cannot receive them, and thus one is prevented from attaining the Path as one ought to.
Sixth, there may be times when one is deaf; being unable to hear, one cannot receive [the teaching], and thus one is prevented from attaining the Path as one ought to."
"Seventh, at times one may be mute, unable to receive [the teaching] and unable to recite it, thereby preventing one from attaining the Way.
Eighth, at times one may have heard [the teaching], yet be unable to receive it, thereby preventing one from attaining the Way."
"Ninth, sometimes those who have not yet attained clarity lack the intention to open [others' minds] by preaching the sutras, thereby preventing them from attaining the Way.
This is the nineteenth dharma.
To personally realize and know that there is no cessation."

What are the nine? First, the cessation of the suffering of names; second, the cessation of the six sense bases; third, the cessation of further craving; fourth, the cessation of sensation; fifth, the cessation of thirst; sixth, the cessation of feeling; seventh, the cessation of the seeking for existence; eighth, the cessation of birth; and ninth, the cessation of old age and death.
These are the ninety dharmas for the practitioner.
They are not false, they are not otherwise; they are true and such as they are, unconfused and non-perverted. This is the contemplation of the mind with wisdom as it truly is.
"The first ten dharmas greatly increase the Path;
they are for those who can preserve the Dharma and provide protection for the Dharma.
What are these ten? "
First, if a disciple of the Way receives [the teaching] from the Tathāgata, it is established according to the root of faith such that no one can destroy it—
not a śramaṇa, nor a brāhmaṇa, nor a deva, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor anyone else in the world.

"Second is the practice of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), which involves upholding the Vinaya, being able to discern the proper spheres of conduct, and seeing offenses according to one's apprehension of fear, training in accordance with the instructions.
Third is having wise friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), following those with wisdom, and associating with those who possess wisdom."
"Fourth is solitary sitting and reflection, practicing with dual restraint: restraint of the body and restraint of the mind.
Fifth is proceeding with refined vigor, possessing vision and strength, fully practicing without abandoning the pure dharmas of skillful means."

"Sixth is the guarding of the mind: dwelling in the most subtle state of mind, one follows what has been done from afar; regarding what is taught, one is able to recollect it and grasp its meaning. Seventh is the practice of wisdom:

arising from the wisdom of origination and cessation, those who follow and attain the Path will certainly have no doubts; they simply act to bring about the destruction of suffering and its extinction."
“Eighth is receiving well-spoken words, which means practicing in accordance with the words of the sublime Dharma.
Ninth is delighting in hearing the Dharma, which means delighting in the practice of hearing the Dharma and taking pleasure solely in frequent preaching of the Dharma.”
"Ten is that which serves as a companion for fellow practitioners, able to provide physical assistance in the practice of diligence.
These are the ten methods of rescue.

Subsequently, one binds oneself through faith, precepts, and wisdom, sitting alone in contemplation; the practitioner’s diligence, intention, and wisdom receive well-spoken words and the desire to preach the sūtras; their physical conduct remains constant and unceasing—this is called 'rescue'."
"The twentieth dharma:
there are ten kinds of straightness that can be practiced.
What are these forms of straightness?
First is right view: through it, the practitioner’s practice of wrong views is eliminated;
furthermore, through various non-unitary conditions of wrong views, the many kinds of evil conduct that arise are able to be eliminated;
and furthermore, through various non-unitary conditions of right view, the many kinds of wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to the fulfillment of practice.
"Second is the reckoning of upright reflection, which eliminates false reckonings;
furthermore, from the various causes and conditions of false reckonings, numerous evil and corrupt practices arise, which this [reckoning] is able to eliminate;
likewise, from the various causes and conditions of upright reflection, numerous wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to their practice and full cultivation."
"Third is direct speech, which eliminates deviant speech;
furthermore, because the causes and conditions for deviant speech are manifold, it can eliminate the various kinds of corrupt and evil conduct that arise from them;
likewise, because the causes and conditions for direct speech are manifold, it brings about the attainment and full practice of various wholesome dharmas."
"Fourth is right conduct (*ṛjuka-carita*), which eliminates wrong conduct (*mithyā-carita*);
furthermore, from various non-unitary causes and conditions of wrong conduct, various evil deeds arise, which it is able to eliminate;
likewise, from various non-unitary causes and conditions of right conduct, various wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to the fulfillment of practice."
"Five are the right actions that eliminate wrong actions;
furthermore, from the various non-unitary causes and conditions of wrong actions, the many kinds of evil conduct that arise can be eliminated;
likewise, from the various non-unitary causes and conditions of right actions, the many kinds of wholesome dharmas are brought forth through the completion of practice."
"The sixth is right exertion (*samyak-pradhāna*), which eliminates wrong exertion;
furthermore, through various non-unitary causes and conditions of wrong exertion, various evil and corrupt practices arise, which it is able to eliminate;
likewise, through various non-unitary causes and conditions of right exertion, various wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to the fulfillment of practice."
"Seventh is right mindfulness, which eliminates wrong mindfulness;
furthermore, through various non-unitary causes and conditions of wrong mindfulness, various evil and unwholesome deeds arise, which it can eliminate;
likewise, through various non-unitary causes and conditions of right mindfulness, various wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to their attainment and full practice."
“Eighth is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), which eliminates wrong concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*);
furthermore, from the various non-unitary causes and conditions of wrong concentration, various evil and corrupt practices arise, which it is able to eliminate;
likewise, from the various non-unitary causes and conditions of right concentration, various wholesome dharmas are brought forth, leading to the fulfillment of practice.”
"Ninth is the direct crossing, which eliminates the crooked crossing;
furthermore, because the causes and conditions for the crooked crossing are manifold, the various evil and corrupt practices that arise can be eliminated;
likewise, because the causes and conditions for the direct crossing are manifold, the various wholesome dharmas are brought forth through the completion of practice."
"Tenth is upright wisdom, which eliminates perverse wisdom;
it can also eliminate the various evil deeds that arise from numerous causes and conditions of perverse wisdom.
Furthermore, through numerous causes and conditions of upright wisdom, one attains the full practice of various wholesome dharmas."
"The thirtieth dharma:
one should thoroughly understand the ten internal and external sense bases of form (*rūpāyatana*). What are these ten?..."

First is the eye-base; second is the form-base; third is the ear-base; fourth is the sound-base; fifth is the nose-base; sixth is the odor-base; seventh is the tongue-base; eighth is the taste-base; ninth is the body-base; and tenth is the coarse-and-subtle base.
“The fortieth dharma:
one should abandon the ten inner and outer hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). What are these ten?

First is the hindrance of internal desire, and second is the hindrance of external desire; when these are fully present, there is neither wisdom nor understanding, and one does not attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world.
"Third is ill will; fourth is the sign of ill will.

Whether it be ill will itself, which is an obscuration, or the sign of ill will, which is also an obscuration—when these are fully present, one does not attain wisdom, nor does one attain liberation, nor does one attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world."
“Fifth is drowsiness; sixth is lethargy.

Whether it be drowsiness or lethargy, each is an obscuration. When these are fully present, one does not attain wisdom, nor does one attain liberation, nor does one attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world.”
“Seventh is resentment (*kukkucca*), and eighth is doubt (*vicikicchā*).

Whether it be resentment, that too is an obscuration; whether it be doubt, that too is an obscuration. When these are fully present, one does not attain wisdom, nor does one attain liberation, nor does one attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world.”

"Nine is doubt regarding wholesome dharmas, and ten is doubt regarding unwholesome dharmas. Whether it be doubt regarding wholesome dharmas or doubt regarding unwholesome dharmas, each is likewise an obscuration. When these are fully present, one does not attain wisdom, nor does one attain understanding, nor does one attain the unconditioned transcendence of the world."
“The fiftieth dharma is that which can cause the ten types of unwholesome conduct to diminish. What are these ten?
[The ten items follow.]”

First is killing; second is stealing; third is sexual misconduct; fourth is double-tongued speech; fifth is lying; sixth is harsh speech; seventh is frivolous speech; eighth is delusion; ninth is anger; tenth is wrong view.
“The sixtieth dharma:
practicing many tenfold pure conducts.
What are these ten? [They are:]”

First, to abandon killing and desist from killing; second, to abandon stealing and desist from stealing; third, to abandon sexual misconduct and desist from sexual misconduct; fourth, to abandon divisive speech and desist from divisive speech; fifth, to abandon false speech and desist from false speech; sixth, to abandon harsh speech and desist from harsh speech; seventh, to abandon frivolous speech and desist from frivolous speech; eighth, to abandon delusion and desist from delusion; ninth, to abandon anger and desist from anger; tenth, to abandon wrong intention and desist from wrong intention.
"The seventieth dharma is difficult to receive:
to fully realize the path that abides in the ten virtues."
What are the ten? First, having abandoned the five kinds;

second, the six factors of right path; third, guarding the one; fourth, relying on the four; fifth, being self-liberated and no longer depending on liberation by others; sixth, having abandoned seeking; seventh, that which was sought being already purified; eighth, bodily activity having ceased; ninth, verbal activity having ceased; tenth, mental activity having ceased.
One whose resolve is supreme, whose wisdom is supreme, and who is complete in conduct is called a "Supreme Person.
This is the eightieth dharma.
It brings to completion the ten universal concentrations.
What are the ten?
First, for a bhikṣu who abides [in this state], the earth is everywhere, above and below, pervasive, non-dual, and immeasurable.
Second, for a bhikṣu who practices, water is everywhere, above and below, pervasive, non-dual, and immeasurable.
"Third, for the practicing bhikṣu, fire is all-pervading above and below, non-dual, and immeasurable.
Fourth, for the practicing bhikṣu, wind is all-pervading above and below, non-dual, and immeasurable."
"5. For the practitioner bhikṣu, there is the color blue, pervading everywhere above and below, non-dual and immeasurable.
6. For the practitioner bhikṣu, there is the color yellow, pervading everywhere above and below, non-dual and immeasurable."
"Seventh is the practitioner monk who is red, pervading everywhere from top to bottom, non-dual, and immeasurable.
Eighth is the practitioner monk who is white, pervading everywhere from top to bottom, non-dual, and immeasurable."
"Ninth, for the practitioner bhikṣu, space is all-pervasive above and below, non-dual, and immeasurable.
Tenth, for the practitioner bhikṣu, consciousness is all-pervasive above and below, non-dual, and immeasurable."
"The Ten Powers of the Buddha.
What are these ten powers?

First, the Buddha possesses knowledge of what is possible as it truly is, and what is impossible as it truly is; he knows what is appropriate and what is inappropriate as it truly is. Through the practice of wisdom, he attains self-knowledge; this is the first power."

"Second, the Buddha possesses knowledge as it truly is regarding the origins and the seeds of calamity for those who have committed offenses in the past, future, and present; this is the second power.

Third, the Buddha possesses knowledge as it truly is regarding the places where all beings dwell and the practices they undertake; through his own transformative wisdom and conduct, he knows this; this is the third power."

"Fourth, the Buddha knows the practice of meditative concentration through its abandonment and understanding, and he also knows from what it is bound, from what it is liberated, and how it arises; these constitute the four powers."
"Fifth, the Buddha possesses such knowledge regarding the various intentions of other families and other individuals; this is the fifth power.
Sixth, the Buddha possesses such knowledge regarding the various and immeasurable types of conduct in the world; this is the sixth power."
"Seventh, the Buddha possesses knowledge regarding whether the faculties of others are complete or incomplete; this is the seventh power.
Eighth, the Buddha possesses knowledge regarding the immeasurable distinctions of past lives, from their very origins up to the present, as he recollects them; this is the eighth power."
"Ninth, the Buddha possesses the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans; he perceives beings coming and going, dying and being born, with full knowledge—this is the ninth power."

"Tenth, the Buddha has exhausted all fetters and latent tendencies; his mind is liberated, and through wisdom he has attained liberation of conduct. Having realized the Dharma through his own insight, he further knows that feeling has ceased and ended, birth is finished, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further coming or going in the world—he has transcended the world. Such is his knowledge; this is the tenth power."
"The ninety-first dharma: one personally realizes and knows that the ten trainings are complete and there is nothing further to learn.
What are these ten?
First, right view is complete, and there is no further training in right view."
"Second, one considers that direct reflection is sufficient and no longer trains in direct reflection.
Third, one declares that direct speech is sufficient and no longer trains in direct speech."
"Fourth, having perfected right conduct, one no longer trains in right conduct.
Fifth, having perfected right action, one no longer trains in right action."
"Sixth, right effort being fulfilled, one no longer trains in right effort.
Seventh, right mindfulness being fulfilled, one no longer trains in right mindfulness."
"Eighth, having perfected right concentration, one no longer trains in right concentration.
Ninth, having attained right transcendence of the world, one no longer trains in right transcendence of the world."
"Tenth, having perfected straightforward wisdom (*ṛju-prajñā*), one no longer trains in straightforward wisdom.
These are the hundred dharmas for the practitioner, explained as a hundredfold teaching.
This is not false, not different; it is true and suchness, unconfused and non-erroneous. This is the contemplation of the mind with wisdom, held according to reality."

"Regarding what has been stated above concerning the teacher who preaches the Dharma: his initial discourse is pure, his intermediate discourse is pure, and his concluding summary is pure; it is beneficial, excellent, complete, and brings about the fulfillment of the pure practice that has been seen. These are called the ten factors of retribution (*daśa-ānuśaṃsā-dharmāḥ*). It is for this reason that what was stated above is taught."
Śāriputra said, "The exposition is now complete; those whose minds were attached to sensory perceptions have received this grace.
